title: Chicken rice hawker says he can't afford overseas holidays, son plays chess with friend at coffeeshop instead
text:
Chicken rice hawker says he can't afford overseas holidays, son plays chess with friend at coffeeshop instead - Mothership.SG - News from Singapore, Asia and around the world 
 ">
News
 Chicken rice hawker says he can't afford overseas holidays, son plays chess with friend at coffeeshop instead
 Commenters expressed their support, calling it "heartwarming" and "wholesome".
 Nicolas Wong 
 November 20, 2026, 08:36 PM
Photos from Poh Kee Chicken Rice/Facebook
 A hawker in Toa Payoh shared a small slice of his son's life on Facebook but unexpectedly gained traction online. 
 The owner of Poh Kee Chicken Rice shared on Nov. 19 that he could not bring his son overseas for the holidays, dubbing himself and his wife "poor hawker parents". 
 Instead, his son brought his friend to the coffeeshop to play chess together while they snacked on chicken nuggets and fries. 
 He later clarified in the caption that the boy in the picture was his own son, lest others misunderstand that he was commenting on others. 
 He added: "I am talking about myself, not judging anyone else..." 
 The hawker also elaborated on his frugal lifestyle in the comment section. 
 "every time we think about travelling and when we calculate, we dare not proceed. In a work year, the off days we take for medical and other purposes are already costing a bomb. I dunno how other can do it, so I guess it's just me who is bad at managing financially...."
 A form of happiness
 Despite the self-deprecating tone, netizens expressed support for him, calling it "heartwarming". 
 Some users agreed that a day spent enjoying games and food with a friend would already mean a lot to a child. 
 One praised his son for spending time with friends and playing chess, saying that it was better than using social media or watching online videos. 
 Other users attempted to reassure the owner, telling him that he did not have to feel lesser for not being able to bring his son on a holiday. 
 "Money can't buy these precious moments," one wrote. 
 Another comment affirmed, "You've brought him up well."
